lede: A scatter graph shows a trend; a line of best fit turns that trend into a rule you can use. On this paper the line always passes through one special point, the mean point. From it you find the line's equation and use it to estimate, as long as you stay inside the data.
can: Find the mean point and draw the line of best fit through it
Find the equation of the line from two points on it
Use the equation to estimate, and say when an estimate cannot be trusted

text: One line through the middle of the data

md:
A community garden records the hours of sunshine each week and the kilograms of tomatoes picked. More sun, more tomatoes: the crosses rise from left to right, but they do not sit exactly on a line.
A line of best fit is the straight line that follows that trend as closely as it can. Once it is drawn, its equation estimates the crop for weeks nobody recorded.

caption: Eight weeks of sunshine and tomatoes. The ringed point is the mean point, and the line passes through it.

prompt: On the scatter graph above, how many weeks are plotted?
explain: 8, one cross for each week. The ringed point is not a week: it is the mean point, which comes next.

md:
Work out $\bar{x}$, the mean of the $x$ values, and $\bar{y}$, the mean of the $y$ values. Together they make the mean point $(\bar{x}, \bar{y})$.
Here the eight sunshine totals add up to 240, so $\bar{x} = 30$, and the eight masses add up to 51.2, so $\bar{y} = 6.4$.

title: Why the mean point?
md: The mean point is the centre of balance of the data: a sensible line through it has the crosses above it balancing the crosses below. It is also the one point on the line you can calculate exactly, so this specification says the line must go through it, and the mark scheme checks that it does.

prompt: Five values of $x$ are 12, 15, 17, 20 and 26. What is $\bar{x}$?
explain: $\dfrac{12 + 15 + 17 + 20 + 26}{5} = \dfrac{90}{5} = 18$. The mean point needs this for $x$ and again for $y$.

text: 2. Draw the line through the mean point

md:
Plot the mean point, then lay your ruler through it along the trend, so that roughly as many crosses lie above the line as below it.
The line does not have to start at the origin, and it usually should not: forcing it through $(0, 0)$ tips it away from the data, even when it still passes through the mean point.

prompt: On the graph with lines A and B, which is the line of best fit?
options: Either, because both pass through the mean point
explain: Line A follows the crosses, four above and four below. Line B was forced through the origin, so it runs below the crosses on the left and above them on the right, even though it also passes through the mean point.

text: 3. The gradient, from two points on your line

md:
Use the mean point and a second point read off your line, well away from it. Never use two plotted crosses: they are data, not points on the line.
Here the line also passes through $(44, 8.5)$, so $m = \dfrac{8.5 - 6.4}{44 - 30} = \dfrac{2.1}{14} = 0.15$. Take both subtractions in the same order and the sign looks after itself.

title: Drawing the line of best fit
why: A short demonstration of drawing a line of best fit by eye. On this paper, make sure yours also passes through the mean point.

prompt: A line of best fit passes through the mean point $(20, 50)$ and the point $(30, 35)$. What is its gradient?
explain: $\dfrac{35 - 50}{30 - 20} = \dfrac{-15}{10} = -1.5$. The line falls from left to right, so its gradient must be negative.

text: 4. The intercept, from the mean point

md:
Substitute the mean point and your gradient into $y = mx + c$, then **subtract** to find $c$:
$6.4 = 0.15 \times 30 + c$, so $c = 6.4 - 4.5 = 1.9$, and the line is $y = 0.15x + 1.9$.
Do not read $c$ off the graph: exam graphs often start their axes above zero, so the line meets the printed axis somewhere other than $x = 0$.

title: Subtract, do not divide
md: Examiners have reported $c$ found by dividing, as if $6.4 \div 4.5$ gave it, instead of subtracting, and intercepts read off graphs whose axes did not start at zero.

prompt: A line of best fit has gradient 2.5 and passes through the mean point $(8, 30)$. What is $c$?
explain: $30 = 2.5 \times 8 + c = 20 + c$, so $c = 30 - 20 = 10$. Dividing $30$ by $20$ would give $1.5$, which is not how an equation is solved.

text: 5. Using the equation, and where to stop

md:
To estimate, substitute into the equation. For 36 hours of sunshine, $y = 0.15 \times 36 + 1.9$.
That is **interpolation**: 36 lies inside the recorded range, 18 to 44 hours, so the estimate can be trusted. For 60 hours you would be **extrapolating** beyond the data, where nobody knows whether the trend carries on, so that estimate cannot be trusted.

prompt: Use $y = 0.15x + 1.9$ to estimate the mass of tomatoes, in kilograms, for a week with 36 hours of sunshine.
explain: $0.15 \times 36 + 1.9 = 7.3$ kg. The estimate comes from the line, not from the nearest cross.

prompt: The garden's line is used to estimate the crop for a week with 60 hours of sunshine. Why is that estimate unreliable?
options: 60 hours is outside the range of the data
The line does not pass through the origin
answer: 60 hours is outside the range of the data
explain: The data run from 18 to 44 hours. Beyond that, nothing shows the trend continues, so using the line there is extrapolation.

md:
Calculate $\bar{x}$ and $\bar{y}$ and plot the mean point.
Draw the line through the mean point along the trend, never forced through the origin.
Find the gradient from two points on your line, one of them the mean point.
Find $c$ by substituting the mean point into $y = mx + c$ and subtracting.
Estimate inside the range of the data, and say why beyond it is extrapolation.

This is usually the second half of the Spearman question: the two means for a mark each, your line drawn through the mean point on the printed graph for two, then its equation for three. The first marks are for the mean point and a line through it; the last is the equation itself. When stuck, find the gradient from the mean point and one other point on your line, then substitute the mean point to find c.
